The proposed WaveletAE model outperforms state-of-the-art time series anomaly detection methods like LSTM encoder-decoder and FCNN on a real-world wind turbine SCADA dataset.

WaveletAE achieves an accuracy of 0.493, precision of 0.471, recall of 0.986, and F1 score of 0.637 in the semi-supervised setting, compared to the LSTM encoder-decoder baseline's 0.428 accuracy, 0.437 precision, 0.928 recall, and 0.594 F1 score.

In the supervised setting, WaveletAE's performance improves further, reaching an accuracy of 0.873, precision of 0.857, recall of 0.863, and F1 score of 0.861, outperforming the LSTM encoder-decoder and FCNN baselines.
The proposed sliding window voting schema allows WaveletAE to make incremental predictions and improve robustness, with the voting threshold τ determining the trade-off between precision and recall.
Traditional methods of installing physical icing detectors on wind turbine blades are limited by high costs, energy consumption, and unreliable sensor readings.
WaveletAE avoids the need for physical icing detectors by analyzing the multivariate SCADA signals, without requiring any mechanical changes to the wind turbine.
The WaveletAE architecture combines wavelet decomposition, convolutional encoders, and LSTM encoders to capture complex channel-wise and temporal patterns in the SCADA data.
Wavelet detail coefficients are used to augment the original SCADA signals, allowing WaveletAE to extract information in both time and frequency domains.
The convolutional encoder in WaveletAE learns global correlations among the signal channels, while the LSTM encoder-decoder captures temporal dynamics.
The reconstruction loss and classification loss are combined in the supervised setting to improve WaveletAE's performance compared to using only reconstruction error.
Increasing the voting threshold τ in the sliding window schema leads to higher precision but lower recall in WaveletAE's predictions.
The sliding window voting schema can enable low-latency monitoring and incremental updates to the icing detection results in real-time deployment.
Wind turbines located in high-altitude areas with a high probability of ice occurrence can experience up to 25% annual energy production losses due to blade icing.
Ice accumulation on wind turbine blades can cause degradation of aerodynamic performance, measurement errors, mechanical failures, and electrical failures.
The SCADA dataset used in the study was provided by Goldwind Inc, one of the world's largest wind turbine manufacturers.
